statement: Five dots are drawn: the four corners of a square and the centre of the square. How many triangles have all three of their corners on these dots?

choices.misconception: I counted only the triangles made from corners of the square and forgot the ones that use the centre.
I noticed that one diagonal gives three dots in a straight line, but forgot that the other diagonal does too.
I counted every way to choose 3 of the 5 dots, but three dots on a diagonal make a straight line, not a triangle.
I counted each triangle that uses the centre twice, once from each of its two square corners.

hints: Split the triangles into those that use the centre and those that do not.
Casework: count the triangles made from three corners, then the triangles made from the centre and two corners. Watch out for three dots that lie on one straight line.
Three corners: 4 triangles. The centre and two corners: 6 pairs of corners, but the 2 pairs of opposite corners lie on a straight line through the centre, so only 4 triangles. Total 4 + 4 = 8.

solutions.reliable: Case 1, no centre: choosing 3 of the 4 corners is the same as leaving one corner out, so there are 4 triangles. Case 2, with the centre: choose 2 corners, which can be done in 6 ways. Opposite corners lie on a diagonal through the centre, so those 2 choices make straight lines, not triangles. That leaves 4. Total 4 + 4 = 8. The transferable idea: split the count into cases and check each case for choices that do not really work.
solutions.elegant: There are 10 ways to choose 3 of the 5 dots. Only the 2 diagonals put three dots in a line, so there are 10 - 2 = 8 triangles.

whyOnTest: Casework with a catch: three dots on a line make no triangle, and spotting the two diagonals is what separates the right count from 10.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
